218.title: Om tat sat (17.23–17.28)
218.hook: three short words that begin and bless an action
218.howItsDone: Some Hindus say 'om tat sat' at the close of a reading, a ritual or a teaching; some printed Gitas set the three words in each chapter's closing line, and verse 17.24 says Vedic rites begin with om.

segments.voice: Yesterday: food, sacrifice, austerity, gift, three kinds each. Your line was which kind. Did you ask it at a meal? Today, three words that close the chapter. Day two hundred eighteen.

Before a runner starts, she touches the line. Before a pianist plays, a breath, hands in the lap. Before a family eats, some pause, some say a word. People mark the start of things that matter. Chapter seventeen has spent a whole day sorting actions into three kinds. Now, at the very end, it offers three words, not for sorting, but for beginning. Om. Tat. Sat. You've already met the first one. It was your second word, back in camp one, the sound before words.
screen: `TOUCH THE LINE.` → `A BREATH BEFORE THE FIRST NOTE.` → `THREE WORDS TO BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-three. Om tat sat: this is remembered as the threefold name of Brahman, the ultimate. By it, long ago, the priests, the Vedas and the sacrifices were set in order. Then Krishna explains each word. Om first. Verse twenty-four: so those who follow the Veda always begin their acts of sacrifice, giving and discipline by saying om. The sound goes first. Tat means that. Verse twenty-five: with tat, people seeking freedom do their sacrifice, discipline and giving without aiming at the reward. It's a way of saying, this isn't for me; it's for that. And sat means real, true, good. Verse twenty-six: sat is used for what is real and what is good, and for any praiseworthy act. Verse twenty-seven: steadiness in sacrifice, discipline and giving is called sat, and so is any action done for its sake. So the three words make a small arc. Om: begin with the sacred sound. Tat: offer it to that, not to yourself. Sat: let it be real and good. And then the chapter's last verse, twenty-eight, is a warning that ties back to faith. Whatever is offered, given or practiced without faith is called asat, unreal. It counts for nothing, here or after. The Sanskrit prefix a means not, so asat is simply not-sat. Some printed editions also set these three words in each chapter's closing line, a way of handing the chapter back. That's the word today: om tat sat.
screen: `THE THREEFOLD NAME.` · `OM: BEGIN WITH THE SOUND.` · `TAT: FOR THAT, NOT FOR ME.` · `SAT: REAL AND GOOD.` · then, large: `OM TAT SAT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one thing you'll do after this. Something ordinary. Cooking, a call, a task at work. Take the first breath as om: the beginning, the sound before words. Take the second as tat: this isn't only for me. Take the third as sat: may it be real and good. If you'd like, you can say the three words softly. Then just sit, and let the action wait. The bell holds the time.
Om tat sat. Gita seventeen, twenty-three: the threefold name of the ultimate. Om, the sacred sound; tat, that; sat, the real and good.
Your line: om tat sat. Before one ordinary task today, pause for three breaths: begin, offer, make it real. Day two hundred eighteen.

fork.reveal: tat, that. seekers of freedom act with tat, without aiming at the reward.

219.title: Renunciation vs relinquishment (18.1–18.12)
219.hook: the last chapter opens with Arjuna asking the difference between two kinds of giving up
219.carry: let go of the fruit, not the act
219.howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors sannyasis, renunciants who leave household life, and it also teaches householders the Gita's tyaga: doing one's duties fully while letting go of attachment to results.

segments.voice: Yesterday: om tat sat. Begin with the sound, offer it to that, let it be real and good. Your line was om tat sat. Today we open the last chapter of the Gita, the graduation chapter. Day two hundred nineteen.

Some people, when life gets hard, want to walk away from all of it. Quit the job, delete the apps, move to a cabin, done. And some people keep showing up to everything, but inside they've quietly stopped needing it to go their way. From the outside, the first one looks like the spiritual one. Chapter eighteen begins with Arjuna asking about exactly this. It's Arjuna's last question in the whole Gita, and it goes all the way back to where he started: wanting to drop his bow and walk off the field.
screen: `WALK AWAY FROM IT ALL?` → `OR STAY, AND STOP GRIPPING?` → `ARJUNA'S LAST BIG QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Verse one: Arjuna asks to know the truth of two words. Sannyasa, renunciation, and tyaga, relinquishment. Both mean giving up. Verse two: the wise say sannyasa is giving up actions done out of desire. And tyaga, they say, is giving up the fruit of all actions. Verse three admits people disagree. Some thinkers say all action has faults, so give it all up. Others say sacrifice, giving and discipline should never be given up. Then Krishna gives his own view, verse five: sacrifice, giving and discipline should not be abandoned. They should be done. They purify the wise. Verse six: but even these should be done without attachment, and without clinging to the fruit. This is my firm conclusion. Then the three threads come back, now applied to giving up. Verse seven: quitting your proper duty out of confusion is tamasic. Verse eight: quitting because it's hard, or you're afraid of the strain, is rajasic, and it gets you nothing. Verse nine: doing your duty because it should be done, while letting go of attachment and the fruit, that's sattvic relinquishment. And verse eleven says it plainly. No one with a body can give up action completely. But the one who gives up the fruit of action, that one is called a relinquisher. So the Gita's answer to the man who wanted to throw down his bow is not walk away. It's stay, act, and let go of the outcome. The same teaching as chapter two, now in its final form. That's the word today: renunciation vs relinquishment.
screen: `SANNYASA AND TYAGA.` · `DON'T DROP THE GOOD WORK.` · `QUITTING FROM FEAR GETS NOTHING.` · `NO ONE CAN STOP ACTING.` · then, large: `RENUNCIATION VS RELINQUISHMENT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one duty you'd love to quit. Something you do because it's yours to do, but it's heavy. Notice the urge to drop it. Is it confusion, or fear of the strain? Don't decide anything. Now picture doing it tomorrow, fully, but without needing it to turn out a particular way. Feel the difference in your shoulders. That's relinquishment. The bell holds the time.
Renunciation vs relinquishment. Gita eighteen: sannyasa gives up actions; tyaga gives up the fruit, and Krishna's firm conclusion is to keep acting and let go of the fruit.
Your line: let go of the fruit, not the act. Do one duty today fully, and let the result be whatever it turns out to be. Day two hundred nineteen.

options: keep acting, without attachment or clinging to the fruit.

trapdoor: what you thought: the spiritual move is to quit everything.
what it means: the Gita says keep doing what's yours to do, and let go of the fruit.
what a scholar hears: 18.2 distinguishes sannyasa (giving up kamya karma, desire-driven acts) from tyaga (giving up karma-phala); 18.7–18.9 sort tyaga by the three gunas.

220.title: Five causes of action (18.13–18.18)
220.hook: every action you take has five causes, and you're only one of them
220.tomorrow: Three kinds of knowledge, action, doer (18.19–18.28)
220.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 18.13–18.16 to loosen the sense of being the sole doer, so that success doesn't feed pride and failure doesn't crush; some devotees offer the results of their actions to God for the same reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday: renunciation vs relinquishment. Keep acting, let go of the outcome. Your line was let go of the fruit, not the act. Did you do one duty without gripping the result? Day two hundred twenty.
screen: `LET GO OF THE FRUIT, NOT THE ACT.`

segments.voice: The exam that went well. The meal that came out right. The moment the right words came for a friend. Was that all one person? There was a body that worked that day. Eyes and hands. Years of practice. And maybe something nobody can name: the right question on the paper, the ripe tomatoes at the market, the friend being ready to hear it. Chapter eighteen takes any action at all and counts its causes. It finds five. And the doer is only one.
screen: `THE THING THAT WENT WELL.` → `WAS IT ALL ONE PERSON?` → `THE GITA COUNTS FIVE CAUSES.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen: learn from me the five causes for the completion of every action, as taught in the Samkhya teaching. Verse fourteen lists them. First, adhishthana, the seat: the body, the base where the action happens. Second, karta, the doer: the one who says I'm doing this. Third, the various instruments: the senses and the mind. Fourth, the many different efforts: the movements, the breaths, the energies that actually carry the action out. And fifth, daiva. Daiva is hard to translate. It can mean the divine, providence, or what some call fate or luck: the part that's beyond your control. Different teachers read it differently, some as God's hand, some as the weight of past karma. Verse fifteen: whatever action a person begins with body, speech or mind, right or wrong, these five are its causes. And verse sixteen is the turn. So the one who sees themselves as the only doer, because their understanding is untrained, doesn't see. The doer is one cause among five. Some teachers say this cuts two ways. When things go well, it takes the air out of pride: you had help, from your body, your senses, your effort, and something beyond all of them. And when things go badly, it takes some weight off guilt: not everything was yours to control. Verse eighteen adds a small map: knowing, the known and the knower set action in motion, and the instrument, the act and the doer hold it together. Tomorrow we'll sort those by the three threads. That's the word today: five causes of action.
screen: `FIVE CAUSES FOR EVERY ACTION.` · `SEAT, DOER, INSTRUMENTS, EFFORT.` · `THE FIFTH: DAIVA, BEYOND YOU.` · `WHO SEES ONLY 'I' DOESN'T SEE.` · then, large: `FIVE CAUSES OF ACTION.`

segments.voice: Sit, and take one breath as an action. Notice the five. The seat: your body, sitting. The doer: the sense that I am breathing. The instruments: the nose, the lungs, the attention. The effort: the muscles moving, the air flowing. And the fifth: the part you didn't make and can't explain, that there is air, that you're alive to breathe it. Let the breath keep going on its own. The bell holds the time.
Five causes of action. Gita eighteen, fourteen: the seat, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and daiva, the unseen fifth. The doer is only one of five.
Your line: not I alone. Today, when something goes well, name one other cause. When something goes wrong, name one too. Day two hundred twenty.

screen: `DAY 220 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE KINDS OF KNOWLEDGE, ACTION, DOER.`

what it means: every action has five causes, and the doer is only one of them.

221.title: Three kinds of knowledge, action, doer (18.19–18.28)
221.hook: the Gita sorts how you see, what you do, and who you are while doing it
221.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 18.19–18.28 as a mirror for work and study: aiming for sattvic knowledge, action and doing, steady, unattached and unshaken by success or failure.

segments.voice: Yesterday: five causes of action. The seat, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and the unseen fifth. Your line was not I alone. Did you name another cause today? Now, the three threads, one more time. Day two hundred twenty-one.

Three people get the same assignment. One looks at it and sees how it fits into something larger. One sees only their own part, and fights to protect it. One grabs a single detail, decides that's the whole thing, and stops thinking. Same task. Three ways of seeing it. Then they do the work: one steadily, one frantically, one carelessly, putting it off. The Gita has been building to this. Yesterday it counted the causes of action. Today it sorts the knowing, the doing and the doer by the three threads.
screen: `SAME TASK, THREE PEOPLE.` → `THE WHOLE, A PIECE, ONE DETAIL.` → `STEADY, FRANTIC, CARELESS.`

segments.voice: Knowledge first. Verse twenty: sattvic knowledge sees one undying reality in all beings, undivided in the divided. You've heard that before; it's chapter thirteen's one light. Verse twenty-one: rajasic knowledge sees all beings as separate, each its own thing, nothing connecting them. Verse twenty-two: tamasic knowledge clings to one small piece as if it were everything, without reason, without grasping what's true. Then action. Verse twenty-three: sattvic action is what needs doing, done without attachment, without craving or hate, by someone not chasing the fruit. Verse twenty-four: rajasic action is driven by desire or ego, done with enormous strain. Verse twenty-five: tamasic action starts in confusion, with no thought for the consequences, the loss, the harm to others, or even whether you're able. Then the doer. Verse twenty-six: the sattvic doer is free of attachment, doesn't talk about themselves, is full of steadiness and energy, and unchanged by success or failure. Verse twenty-seven: the rajasic doer is passionate, wants the fruit, is greedy, can be harmful, and swings between joy and grief. Verse twenty-eight: the tamasic doer is unsteady, crude, stubborn, deceitful, lazy, gloomy, and dirghasutri. That last word is a compound of dirgha, long, and sutra, thread. Long-threaded: someone who keeps stretching a job out. A procrastinator. So a word for putting things off is sitting in the Gita's last chapter. The chapter goes on to sort understanding, resolve and even happiness the same way. The point isn't to label yourself forever. It's to see which kind you're being right now. That's the word today: three kinds of knowledge.
screen: `SEEING ONE, SEEING MANY, SEEING A BIT.` · `STEADY, STRAINED, OR CARELESS.` · `THE DOER UNCHANGED BY SUCCESS.` · `DIRGHASUTRI: THE PROCRASTINATOR.` · then, large: `THREE KINDS OF KNOWLEDGE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one task waiting for you. Notice how you're seeing it. As part of something bigger? As only your piece? As one annoying detail? Then notice how you'd do it: steadily, frantically, or not at all yet. No judgment. Now picture yourself doing it the steady way, with energy but without needing praise. Hold that picture for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Three kinds of knowledge. Gita eighteen, nineteen to twenty-eight: knowledge, action and the doer each come in three kinds, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic.
Your line: know your kind. Today, pick the one task you've been stretching out, and do the first steady piece of it. Day two hundred twenty-one.

fork.reveal: sattvic: seeing the one in the many (verse 20), and acting without attachment to the fruit (verse 23).

original.note: Sanskrit: dirghasutri, long-threaded (dirgha, long + sutra, thread): the one who drags a task out; Gita 18.28.

what it means: knowledge, action and the doer can each lean clear, restless or heavy, and you can notice which one you're being now.

222.title: Duty according to nature (18.41–18.48)
222.hook: your own path, done badly, beats someone else's done well
222.carry: your own dharma, imperfect, beats another's, perfect
222.howItsDone: Some Hindus understand svadharma as the duties that belong to their own life and stage of life, and offer their daily work as worship; how the Gita's varna verses relate to birth-based caste is still debated among Hindus.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three kinds of knowledge, action and doer, and the long-threaded procrastinator. Your line was know your kind. Did you do the first steady piece? Today, a hard and important passage. Day two hundred twenty-two.

Five minutes of scrolling, and there they are: a dozen lives that look better. Someone's startup, someone's travel, someone's calm morning routine. It's easy to start living their life in your head. Copying their plan, their job, their whole personality. The Gita has a line about this, and it said it once already, back in chapter three. Here in chapter eighteen it comes again, almost word for word: your own dharma, even done imperfectly, is better than someone else's, done perfectly. But the verses around it need care.
screen: `A DOZEN BETTER-LOOKING LIVES.` → `COPYING SOMEONE ELSE'S PATH.` → `YOUR OWN, EVEN IMPERFECT.`

segments.voice: Verses forty-one to forty-four describe the four varnas, the classes of ancient Indian society: brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras. Their work, Krishna says, is divided by the qualities born of their nature. Calm, self-control, learning and faith for brahmins. Courage, skill and generosity for kshatriyas, Arjuna's class of warriors. Farming, cattle and trade for vaishyas. Service for shudras. This is where honesty matters. These verses have been used to support caste as a hierarchy fixed by birth, and people were deeply hurt by it. The reformer B. R. Ambedkar criticized the Gita sharply for this. Some modern Hindu teachers read varna as temperament and calling rather than birth, pointing to chapter four, where Krishna says the four were made by quality and action. Hindus still disagree about this, and the disagreement is real. Then verse forty-five turns to the heart of the passage: a person who is devoted to their own work reaches perfection. Verse forty-six: by worshiping, through their own work, the one from whom all beings come, a person reaches perfection. In this verse, work itself becomes worship. And verse forty-seven: better your own dharma, even imperfect, than another's, even done well. Verse forty-eight adds: don't abandon the work that's yours, even if it has flaws. Every undertaking is wrapped in some fault, the way fire is wrapped in smoke. Whatever one makes of the varna verses, these last four say: find what's truly yours to do, and do it, smoke and all. That's the word today: duty according to nature.
screen: `FOUR VARNAS, BY QUALITY AND WORK.` · `USED TO DEFEND CASTE BY BIRTH.` · `YOUR WORK CAN BE WORSHIP.` · `EVERY FIRE HAS SOME SMOKE.` · then, large: `DUTY ACCORDING TO NATURE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a life you've envied lately. Let it come fully into view. Then gently set it down. Now think of the work that's actually in front of you: your family, your job, your studies, your one small patch of the world. Notice its imperfections. The smoke. Then notice the fire: the part of it that's truly yours, that no one else could do quite the same way. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Duty according to nature. Gita eighteen: svadharma, your own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's done well; your own work can be worship.
Your line: your own dharma, imperfect, beats another's, perfect. Today, when you catch yourself comparing, turn back to one thing that's yours to do, and do it. Day two hundred twenty-two.

options: switch to the life that looks better.

trapdoor: what you thought: this passage is only about caste.
what it means: it names the social order of its time, and teaches that your own path, done imperfectly, is better than borrowing another's.

223.title: The path to Brahman (18.49–18.58)
223.hook: near the end, Krishna draws the whole road in ten verses
223.tomorrow: "I have told you. Now do as you choose." (18.59–18.66)
223.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers read Gita 18.49–18.58 as a summary of the whole spiritual path, from unattached work and disciplined living to realizing Brahman and supreme devotion (para bhakti).

segments.voice: Yesterday: duty according to nature. Your line was your own dharma, imperfect, beats another's, perfect. Every fire has some smoke. Did you turn back to what's yours? Today, where that road leads. Day two hundred twenty-three.

Near the end of a long hike, someone who's walked it before often stops the group at a clearing and points. See that ridge? We came over that. See the river? We crossed it. And there, the summit. That's where we're going. It doesn't make the last stretch shorter, but suddenly the whole trail makes sense. Chapter eighteen has a passage like that. In about ten verses, Krishna draws the whole road, from ordinary work all the way to Brahman, and to love beyond it.
screen: `A CLEARING NEAR THE END.` → `THE RIDGE, THE RIVER.` → `AND THERE, THE SUMMIT.`

segments.voice: Verse forty-nine: with understanding unattached everywhere, self mastered, desire gone, a person reaches through relinquishment the highest perfection, freedom from the bind of action. Verse fifty: now hear, briefly, how the one who's reached that perfection reaches Brahman. Then the road, verses fifty-one to fifty-three. A clear understanding. Holding yourself steady with resolve. Setting aside sound and the other sense objects, putting down liking and disliking. Seeking quiet, solitary places, eating lightly, speech, body and mind held in check. Always turning to meditation, resting in dispassion. Letting go of ego, force, pride, desire, anger, and the need to own things. Free of mine, at peace. That one, Krishna says, is fit to become Brahman. The word that holds it together is dhriti, steadiness, resolve. Not a burst of effort. A steady hand. Then verse fifty-four, the summit, and a surprise. Having become Brahman, serene, that person neither grieves nor craves. The same toward all beings, they reach the highest love for me. One might expect the road to end in a merging where love disappears. Here, on becoming Brahman, love begins. Verse fifty-five: by love they know me as I truly am, and knowing me, they enter me. Advaita teachers read this as knowledge completing itself; Vaishnava teachers read it as devotion as the goal. Both keep the verse. Then Krishna turns to Arjuna. Verse fifty-seven: give all your actions to me in your mind. Verse fifty-eight: with your mind on me, by my grace you'll cross every obstacle. But if, out of ego, you won't listen, you'll be lost. That's the word today: the path to Brahman.
screen: `PERFECTION THROUGH LETTING GO.` · `STEADY: SIMPLE, QUIET, FREE OF MINE.` · `BECOMING BRAHMAN, LOVE BEGINS.` · `BY MY GRACE YOU'LL CROSS.` · then, large: `THE PATH TO BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and try one piece of the road: steadiness. Keep the spine upright and the breath even. When a sound comes, let it pass without liking or disliking it. When a thought of mine comes, my plans, my things, let it pass too. You're not forcing anything. Just holding steady, like a hand around a cup of water, firm but not tight. The bell holds the time.
The path to Brahman. Gita eighteen, forty-nine to fifty-eight: relinquishment, steadiness, a quiet, solitary life free of mine, becoming Brahman, and then the highest love.
Your line: steady. Today, when something pulls you off balance, come back to one steady breath before you respond. Day two hundred twenty-three.

224.title: "I have told you. Now do as you choose." (18.59–18.66)
224.word: "I have told you. Now do as you choose."
224.hook: after seven hundred verses, Krishna hands the decision back to Arjuna
224.tomorrow: "Abandon all dharmas, come to me alone" (18.66–18.72)
224.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often point to Gita 18.63, 'reflect fully, then do as you wish', as a sign that the Gita invites understanding and free choice rather than blind obedience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the path to Brahman, the whole road in ten verses, and love at the summit. Your line was steady. Did one steady breath come before a reply? Today, the most surprising move in the book. Day two hundred twenty-four.

Imagine the best teacher you ever had spending months with you. Every question answered, every doubt heard, and once, a vision that nearly knocked you over. And then, at the very end, instead of saying, so now you must do this, they close the book and say: I've told you everything. Think it over. Then do what you choose. That's what happens in chapter eighteen. God, in the Gita's own story, doesn't command the final move. He hands it back.
screen: `MONTHS OF ANSWERS.` → `ONE OVERWHELMING VISION.` → `THEN: DO AS YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: It starts with a warning. Verse fifty-nine: if, leaning on your ego, you think, I will not fight, that decision is useless. Your own nature will push you to it. Verse sixty: bound by your own work, born of your nature, you'll do helplessly what you, confused, don't want to do. Then verse sixty-one, a strange picture. The Lord lives in the heart of every being, Arjuna, and by his power moves them all, as if they were mounted on a machine. Verse sixty-two: go to him for refuge with your whole being. By his grace you'll reach the highest peace. And then verse sixty-three. So I have told you this wisdom, more secret than any secret. Reflect on it fully. Then do as you wish. Yathecchasi tatha kuru. As you wish, so do. After all the teaching, all the argument, the vision of chapter eleven, Krishna doesn't force a choice. Many readers, especially modern teachers, find this one of the most striking moments in the book. The Gita's God persuades, shows, loves, and then respects Arjuna enough to let him decide. But he doesn't walk away. Verse sixty-four: hear my highest word once more. You are deeply loved by me. Verse sixty-five repeats a line from chapter nine: keep your mind on me, be devoted to me, and you will come to me. I promise you truly, for you are dear to me. So the handing back isn't cold. It comes wrapped in the plainest statement of love in the whole book. This closes the week: om tat sat, relinquishment, five causes, three kinds, your own dharma, steady, and now this. That's the word today: I have told you. Now do as you choose.
screen: `YOUR NATURE WILL MOVE YOU.` · `THE LORD IN EVERY HEART.` · `REFLECT, THEN DO AS YOU WISH.` · `YOU ARE DEEPLY LOVED.` · then, large: `NOW DO AS YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one choice you're facing. Let yourself hear all the advice you've been given about it, from people, from books, from these days. Let it all be said. Then let it go quiet. Now, in the quiet, reflect on it fully, the way verse sixty-three asks. You don't have to decide. Just notice that the choice is yours, and that you can make it without fear. The bell holds the time.
I have told you. Now do as you choose. Gita eighteen, sixty-three: after all the teaching, Krishna says reflect fully, then do as you wish.
